title: Following Delegation Traces to Study Human Oversight in Interaction with Multimodal AI
title_zh: 追踪委托行为：探究人类在与多模态人工智能互动中的监督机制

paragraphs.en: As multimodal AI systems are becoming our everyday thought partners, the shift towards studying how users transfer control to these systems becomes especially urgent. In this paper, we report an overview of findings from an online study with n = 56 n=56 AI-literate participants and 392 Video Question Answering trials. After inspecting each multimodal AI response, participants rated task-specific trust and selected one of three intended policies for an analogous future task: reject AI assistance, use it with verification, or delegate fully to the AI. Within participants, post-interaction trust strongly predicted the user’s delegation choices ( OR = 14.97 \mathrm{OR}=14.97 , 95% CI [ 7.14 , 31.37 ] [7.14,31.37] ). Trust and delegation nevertheless remained distinct. Verification was the dominant policy and often co-occurred with high trust. Delegation also increased with task order after adjustment for momentary and participant-level trust ( OR = 1.22 \mathrm{OR}=1.22 , 95% CI [ 1.02 , 1.45 ] [1.02,1.45] ), indicating an experience-related component that self-reported trust ratings alone could not capture. These findings motivate a shift from intended delegation to a non-intrusive observation of how delegation is enacted in collaborative human-AI tasks. We therefore conclude by proposing enacted delegation traces as a methodological framework for future studies of multimodal and agentic AI use.
paragraphs.zh: 随着多模态人工智能系统逐渐成为我们日常思考的伙伴，研究用户如何向这些系统转移控制权变得尤为紧迫。 在本文中，我们报告了一项在线研究的总体发现，该研究共有 n = 56 名具备人工智能素养的参与者以及 392 次视频问答试验。 在检查每个多模态人工智能的回应后，参与者对任务相关的信任度进行了评分，并从三种预设策略中选择一种用于类似的未来任务：拒绝人工智能协助、在使用时进行验证，或完全将任务委托给人工智能。 在参与者层面，互动后的信任度强烈预测了用户的委托选择（OR = 14.97 \mathrm{OR}=14.97，95% CI [7.14, 31.37]）。 尽管如此，信任与委托仍然是两个独立的概念。 验证是占主导地位的策略，且常与高信任度同时出现。 在控制了瞬时信任和参与者层面的信任因素后，委托行为也随任务顺序的增加而上升（OR = 1.22 \mathrm{OR}=1.22，95% CI [1.02, 1.45]），这表明存在一种与经验相关的因素，是仅靠自我报告的信任评分无法捕捉到的。 这些发现促使我们将研究重点从预期的委托行为转向对人工智能协作任务中实际委托过程的非侵入式观察。 因此，我们在结论中提出将“实际执行的委托痕迹”作为一种方法论框架，用于未来关于多模态和智能体型人工智能使用方式的研究。

paragraphs.en: A typical day in the life of a 2026 knowledge worker may look like this. The day begins in an online meeting, where an AI assistant listens quietly in the background, turning the discussion into notes. Later, while drafting a technical report, they ask another assistant to revise a paragraph and keep only the most useful suggestions. A scientific claim looks useful, but not quite safe to trust, so they verify it against external sources. They also need a chart to accompany the text, so they ask another AI assistant to write the code for generating it, before adding their final touches.

paragraphs.en: Human agency and oversight are central to European frameworks for Trustworthy AI and are explicitly reflected in the AI Act High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence (2019) ; European Parliament and Council of the European Union (2024) . Yet translating these principles into interaction-level evaluation remains an open challenge: technical properties such as transparency, robustness, and accountability Chander et al. (2025) ; Novelli et al. (2024) do not by themselves reveal how users retain or transfer control while working with an AI system. We therefore ask: how can human oversight be made observable in practice while AI carries out part or all of a task?

paragraphs.en: We propose delegation as a complementary lens for studying human oversight as it is enacted in interaction with multimodal AI systems. Delegation concerns which parts of a task users hand over to an AI system, how they inspect or verify its outputs, and when they intervene to change or reclaim control. In this view, a system may satisfy technical and regulatory requirements for trustworthiness while still eliciting poorly calibrated delegation. For instance, a user may trust an AI system while still deciding to verify its output or completely avoid full delegation for tasks they perceive as personally meaningful or risky. The same user, nonetheless, may delegate to a less trusted system when time, fatigue, or lack of expertise makes independent work costly. For this reason, we distinguish: trustworthiness , as the properties of the system and its deployment; trust , as the user’s situated perception of those properties Mayer et al. (1995) ; and delegation , as the observable transfer of control over task execution and decision authority between the human and the AI system Lee and See (2004) . This perspective is also relevant to the Explainable AI (XAI) field: an explanation or inspectable representation can support oversight not only by changing trust, but by shaping how users delegate to the AI the system.
paragraphs.zh: 我们将“委托”视为研究人类在与多模态人工智能系统互动中实施监督的一种补充视角。委托涉及用户将任务的哪些部分交给人工智能系统、他们如何检查或验证系统的输出，以及他们在何时介入以改变或重新夺回控制权。从这一视角来看，一个系统可能满足技术性和监管性的可靠性要求，但仍可能导致未经充分校准的委托行为。例如，用户可能信任一个人工智能系统，但仍决定验证其输出，或者对于他们认为具有个人意义或存在风险的任务，完全避免全面委托。然而，同一位用户也可能在时间紧迫、疲劳或缺乏专业知识导致独立完成任务成本过高时，将任务委托给一个可靠性较低的系统。因此，我们区分了三个概念：可靠性（trustworthiness），即系统及其部署所具备的特性；信任（trust），即用户对这些特性的情境化感知（Mayer et al. (1995)）；以及委托（delegation），即人类与人工智能系统之间在执行任务和决策权限方面可观察到的控制权转移（Lee and See (2004)）。这一视角也与可解释人工智能（XAI）领域相关：解释或可检查的表示不仅可以通过改变信任来支持监督，还可以通过影响用户向该系统进行任务委托的方式来实现。

(2025) ; Mehrotra et al. (2024) ; Gor et al. (2026) . This gap is particularly relevant for multimodal systems, where existing evaluation still focuses predominantly on model performance and user preferences Lee et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2024) ; Lu et al. (2024) ; Chou et al. (2025) rather than on how control is negotiated across repeated interactions.

paragraphs.en: The contribution of this paper is twofold. First, we provide a task-level account of how trust, repeated experience, and the availability of an inspectable graph representation for the model answers relate to intended delegation among AI-literate users, whom we selected as a deliberate first population for studying these dynamics during repeated multimodal interaction (Section 3 and 4). Second, we introduce enacted delegation traces as a general framework for studying how responsibility is redistributed during collaborative tasks across user populations and application contexts (Sections 5 and 6). We formalise these traces through the scope of control transfer, the oversight actions performed after delegation, and the recovery of control. We then outline how these elements may be observed under varying time pressure, perceived AI competence, and task stakes. Experimental results reported in this paper measure intended delegation only; the enacted-delegation framework introduced in Sections 5–6 is a methodological proposal motivated by these findings that has not yet been implemented or validated. Our proposed framing positions delegation as a measurable object for evaluating the quality of oversight supported by multimodal and agentic AI systems.
paragraphs.zh: 本文的贡献有两方面。 首先，我们从任务层面阐述了信任、重复经验以及模型答案的可检查图表示的可用性，如何与具备人工智能素养的用户所期望的委托行为相关联；我们特意选择这类用户作为研究这些动态过程中重复多模态交互的首批对象（第 3 节和第 4 节）。 其次，我们引入了“实际执行委托轨迹”这一通用框架，用于研究在协作任务中，责任如何在不同用户群体和应用场景中被重新分配（第 5 节和第 6 节）。 我们通过控制转移的范围、委托后执行的监督行动以及控制的恢复过程，对这些轨迹进行了形式化描述。 接着，我们概述了在不同时间压力、感知到的 AI 能力水平以及任务重要性条件下，这些要素可能如何被观察到。 本文报告的实验结果仅测量了期望的委托行为；第 5–6 节中提出的实际执行委托框架是一种基于这些发现的方法论提案，目前尚未实施或验证。 我们提出的框架将委托视为一个可测量的对象，用于评估多模态和智能体型 AI 系统所支持监督的质量。

paragraphs.en: In the paper, we use a focused empirical result to motivate a methodological position. Video Question Answering provides a controlled multimodal setting in which users must judge whether an AI system has correctly represented objects, actions, and temporal relations before deciding how much control to retain. From the standpoint of XAI, it also enables a comparison between a textual answer and an editable spatio-temporal graph that exposes part of the represented video situation for inspection. Thus, we designed a repeated Video Question Answering study, where participants rated trust after each response and selected whether they would reject AI assistance, use it with retained control, or delegate fully on an analogous task. Higher-than-usual trust strongly predicted stronger intended delegation, while retained control remained common even at high trust. Exploratory findings further suggest that graph-supported presentation was associated with stronger delegation. Together, these findings show that delegation captures how users allocate oversight across repeated interaction in ways that trust ratings alone leave only partly visible.

paragraphs.en: Trust has long been treated as a central construct for explaining how people use automated systems. In classic accounts, it describes a willingness to accept vulnerability to another actor Mayer et al. (1995) , while appropriate reliance concerns whether users rely on automation when it is capable and withhold reliance when it is not Lee and See (2004) . This distinction is important for human-AI interaction because trust remains a subjective judgement, whereas reliance and delegation become visible in how users allocate control. Delegation is especially relevant for systems that do more than provide advice. Yet empirical work still tends to study the users’ post-interaction reactions to AI recommendations more often than the conditions under which users are prepared to transfer control. Gomez et al., for instance, found delegation in only a small fraction of the human-AI interaction sequences reviewed in their survey Gomez et al. (2025) . Recent studies have begun to operationalise delegation more directly, either through willingness to delegate a repeated perceptual task Mehrotra et al. (2024) , or through behavioural traces of whether teams allow an AI partner to answer on their behalf Gor et al. (2026) . These works motivate measuring delegation as a construct related to trust, but analytically distinct from it.

paragraphs.en: Delegation also connects to established work on human-automation function allocation. Parasuraman et al. distinguish types and levels of automation across information acquisition, analysis, decision selection, and action implementation Parasuraman and Riley (1997) . Pritchett et al. frame function allocation as assigning work across human and automated agents, highlighting potential mismatches between responsibility and authority Pritchett et al. (2014) . (2023) ; Mehrotra et al. (2024) . (2026) .

paragraphs.en: The distinction between reported trust and delegation is particularly underexplored in multimodal AI, compared to language-based AI models and tasks. Research on vision-language models has largely focused on model-centric trustworthiness metrics, including hallucination, robustness, and benchmark performance, while fewer studies examine how users interpret repeated multimodal outputs and translate these evaluations into delegation decisions Chiatti et al. (2025) . Benchmarks such as VHELM and MultiTrust broaden evaluation beyond accuracy by considering several dimensions of multimodal model behaviour Lee et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2024) . Public agent arenas Lu et al. (2024) ; Chou et al. (2025) move closer to situated use by collecting open-ended interactions and preference judgements. However, user preferences do not show how trust evolves across repeated tasks, nor how users retain and transfer their judgment or control over a task. A co-evolutionary view of human-AI interaction further suggests that these choices should be studied across repeated encounters, as both user strategies and system capabilities change through use Pedreschi et al. (2025) .

paragraphs.en: Our enacted-delegation perspective builds on these ongoing efforts by focusing on how control transfer during task execution, answer inspection, and recovery of control unfold behaviourally during interaction. We begin exploring Video Question Answering tasks, where users must assess whether a system has correctly interpreted objects, actions, and temporal relations in a video. The STAR benchmark is well suited to this setting because its questions depend on situated reasoning over structured events Wu et al. (2021) . In such tasks, a fluent textual answer can conceal the intermediate representation on which the answer depends. Graph-based presentations offer one way to expose this intermediate layer by making entities and relations inspectable Mitra et al. (2024) ; Lusha et al. (2025) . In our study, we treat graphs as an interface-level presentation model rather than as a guarantee of correctness. It externalises part of the represented video situation, gives users a concrete object to inspect and edit, and allows us to test the effects of a more interactive interface on self-reported trust and delegation choices.

paragraphs.en: Each retained participant completed one guided practice task followed by exactly seven analytic Video Question Answering trials derived from the STAR benchmark Wu et al. (2021) . The analytic task set comprised the same seven selected STAR sequence items across participants; these required connecting actions occurring at different points in an everyday video and determining their temporal order. System responses were generated in advance with Gemini 2.5 Flash so that participants assigned to the same experimental condition encountered stable and comparable stimuli. We restricted the STAR material to temporal sequence questions because preliminary experiments Lusha et al. (2025) found temporal and predictive questions among the most challenging for the Gemini 2.5 Flash. Since predictive questions in STAR include relevant answer evidence only in the ground-truth graphs, but not in the accompanying video clips, we limited our analysis to sampled temporal questions to enable a fair comparison between text-only and graph-supported variants. In each trial, participants first watched the video and answered the multiple-choice question. They then inspected a response presented as coming from a generic multimodal AI, without knowing any details about the specific model used for generating answers. We tested four different website variants enabling controlled experimental conditions, summarised in Figure 1 . Depending on the group assignment, users were exposed on either text-only answers or text accompanied by an editable spatio-temporal graph. Moreover, two samples served as control group: i.e., users thought they were evaluating AI-generated answers when in fact they were presented with ground truth data. To control for the presence of errors in the AI-generated responses, a later participant cohort encountered deliberately erroneous responses. The present paper does not delve into the analysis of condition effects. Here we simply provide an overview of the pooled effects among trust, intended delegation, and task order, with condition indicators retained as covariates. No a priori or post-hoc power analyses were conducted: small and uneven between-condition samples are treated as exploratory rather than precisely estimated intervention effects.

paragraphs.en: The pooled model predicted the ordered delegation choice from within-person trust, the participant’s mean trust, task order, recruitment cohort, graph presentation, and error-exposure assignment. This model allowed us to separate two levels of variation: between-person differences captured by each participant’s mean post-response trust, and within-person fluctuations captured by trial-level trust relative to that participant’s own mean. We used within-person trust as focal predictor; recruitment cohort, graph presentation, and error exposure were included as adjustment covariates, while task order was retained as an exploratory predictor (Table 2 ). Therefore, the focal coefficient asks whether the same participant selected a stronger policy on trials in which their trust was higher than their personal average. This within-person estimate is important because it reduces the risk of confusing stable individual differences with task-level changes in trust and delegation. We used likelihood-ratio testing to assess whether the focal trust term improved model fit. We also report the association with task order as an exploratory result, since the study was not designed to determine whether changes across the session reflected learning, fatigue, habituation, or growing familiarity with the AI support. Because task order and item identity were confounded in the earlier cohort, we additionally re-estimated the pooled cumulative-logit model including the seven video items as categorical fixed effects. The participant random intercept and all other predictors were unchanged. Since the present paper overviews the study mainly to motivate the transition towards enacted delegation, we provide only a compact analysis of graph presentation alongside the pooled relationships among trust, intended delegation, and task order.

paragraphs.en: The intended delegation item used in the study we just overviewed was task-specific, temporally close to the trust rating, and preserved verification (i.e., delegation with retained control) as an explicit oversight policy. These properties made it useful for showing that trust and delegation can be measured together during repeated multimodal AI interaction. At the same time, the measure remained separated from the collaborative process itself. Participants did not hand over part of the current task, their choice did not alter the workflow, and no performance or effort consequences followed from the selected policy. The verification option also compressed behaviours that may differ substantially in practice, such as briefly checking a salient video segment, reconstructing the answer independently, or correcting an intermediate representation before accepting the AI contribution, for instance.

paragraphs.en: In this framing, self-reported trust remains central as a subjective measure, but it should be positioned as complementary to the delegation trace. This additional recording of trust ratings would reveal regions where self-reported trust and enacted delegation overlap or, more interestingly, diverge. paragraphs.en: Design considerations. The next methodological step is to observe how delegation is enacted while a human and an AI system jointly produce an outcome. As defined in Section 5 , we introduce enacted delegation traces to make observable the transfer of control between human and AI during an ongoing activity. The study we envision should therefore seamlessly integrate delegation as part of the task, rather than an additional question asked after the task has already ended.
paragraphs.zh: 设计考量。 下一个方法论步骤是观察，当人类与人工智能系统共同产生结果时，委托是如何被实施的。 如第 5 节所定义，我们引入“已实施的委托痕迹”，以便在持续活动中观察到人类与人工智能之间的控制转移过程。 因此，我们所设想的这项研究应将委托无缝地整合到任务本身之中，而不是在任务结束后才提出的一个额外问题。

sents.zh: 下一个方法论步骤是观察，当人类与人工智能系统共同产生结果时，委托是如何被实施的。

sents.en: As defined in Section 5 , we introduce enacted delegation traces to make observable the transfer of control between human and AI during an ongoing activity.
sents.zh: 如第 5 节所定义，我们引入“已实施的委托痕迹”，以便在持续活动中观察到人类与人工智能之间的控制转移过程。

sents.en: The study we envision should therefore seamlessly integrate delegation as part of the task, rather than an additional question asked after the task has already ended.
sents.zh: 因此，我们所设想的这项研究应将委托无缝地整合到任务本身之中，而不是在任务结束后才提出的一个额外问题。

paragraphs.en: A promising direction is to extend the Video Question Answering setup into a more realistic and gamified learning scenario. Participants could watch short recorded lessons or tutorials and answer a sequence of questions under varying time constraints. Sample questions may require, for instance, locating a specific moment in the video, reconstructing the order of explained steps, or applying concepts explained in the video to a new case. The number of questions could be feasible in the baseline condition and deliberately difficult in groups where we aim to test the effect of time pressure. The interface must also allow for hybrid delegation scenarios: participants could ask the AI to locate relevant video segments, draft an answer, or produce a short explanation, while still being responsible for the final submitted response.
paragraphs.zh: 一个有前景的方向是将视频问答设置扩展为更真实且更具游戏化的学习场景。 参与者可以观看简短的录播课程或教程，并在不同的时间限制下回答一系列问题。 示例问题可能要求，例如，在视频中定位特定时刻、重建所解释步骤的顺序，或将视频中讲解的概念应用于新案例。 在基准条件下，问题数量可以是合理的；而在旨在测试时间压力效应的组别中，则可以有意识地设置难题。 界面还必须支持混合委托场景：参与者可以要求人工智能定位相关视频片段、草拟答案或生成简短解释，同时仍需对最终提交的答案负责。

paragraphs.en: This task directly extends the empirical study reported in this paper and can initially be applied to the same population of AI-literate university students. This population provides a useful starting point for refining the measures and interaction traces with users already familiar with AI-supported work. At the same time, it is closer to everyday AI use in educational settings, where students increasingly rely on AI systems to summarise lectures and prepare for assessments. However, the framework is general and can be applied to the study of broader populations, e.g., by integrating more informational and general-purpose videos, or workplace training material.
paragraphs.zh: 这项任务直接拓展了本文报告的实证研究，并且最初可以应用于同样具备人工智能素养的大学生群体。 这一群体为完善测量方法和与熟悉人工智能辅助工作的用户之间的互动痕迹提供了一个有用的起点。 同时，这一情境更贴近教育环境中日常的人工智能使用，因为学生越来越依赖人工智能系统来总结课程和准备评估。 然而，该框架具有通用性，可以应用于更广泛群体的研究，例如通过整合更多信息类和通用类视频，或职场培训材料。

paragraphs.en: The interface should instantiate delegation through ordinary workflow actions mimicking real-world use. paragraphs.en: In any case, the interface design should be preceded by a participatory phase. Practical workshops and focus groups can help us identify the situations in which different users already delegate to AI, the moments in which they would like improved and increased oversight of the system. Moreover, there may be key factors shaping delegation in real use beyond time pressure, perceived capability and risk that we may have not anticipated before a focused discussion with users. Users may also respond to boredom, uncertainty about assessment criteria, social norms around acceptable AI use, or effort-related factors, to name just a few. Thus, this participatory phase is instrumental in informing the final task scenarios and control items implemented in the envisaged interface.
paragraphs.zh: 无论如何，界面设计之前都应先进行参与式阶段。 实践工作坊和焦点小组能帮助我们识别不同用户已经将任务委托给人工智能的情形，以及他们希望加强对系统监督的时机。 此外，在真实使用环境中，除了时间压力、感知能力和风险之外，可能还有其他关键因素影响着任务委托，而这些因素或许在我们与用户进行针对性讨论之前尚未被预见。 用户也可能因无聊、对评估标准的不确定、关于可接受人工智能使用的社会规范，或与努力相关的因素而做出反应，这只是其中几个例子。 因此，这一参与式阶段对于明确最终任务场景和拟在预期界面中实施的控制项目至关重要。

paragraphs.en: Modelled conditions. An important requirement for conducting the envisaged study is ensuring that specific experimental controls are in place for factors shaping enacted delegation. One way to approach this requirement is to adopt an approach similar to the experimental setup presented in this paper, where participant groups are assigned to different control conditions while seemingly completing the same task. The first condition to test concerns the AI output presentation mode. Depending on the task, the interface could expose AI outputs structured differently: e.g., from a plain textual answer up until a richer interactive workspace where users can view, edit or reject intermediate outputs. This configuration would extend the graph-presentation manipulation used in the preliminary study, while shifting the role of the representation from an explanation shown after the answer to an object through which the user can supervise the collaboration.
paragraphs.zh: 模拟条件。 开展预期研究的一项重要要求是，确保为影响实际委托过程的因素设置特定的实验对照。 满足这一要求的一种方法是采用与本文提出的实验设置类似的方法：将参与者分组分配到不同的对照条件下，同时表面上完成相同的任务。 首个需要测试的条件涉及人工智能输出的呈现模式。 根据任务的不同，界面可以以不同方式呈现人工智能的输出结果：例如，从简单的文本答案，到更丰富的交互式工作区，用户可以在其中查看、编辑或拒绝中间输出。 这种配置将扩展初步研究中使用的图表呈现操控方法，同时将呈现方式的角色从“答案后展示的解释”转变为“用户可借此监督协作过程的对象”。

One dimension for controlling the AI behaviour is the injection of incorrect and fabricated answers, similar to the error-injected cohort in our preliminary study. Another dimension is to expose users to different levels of proactive suggestion by the AI, to simulate agentic scenarios. Lastly, another interesting but still underexplored dimension concerns the comparison between a static AI system and adapting AI systems that co-evolve with users.

paragraphs.en: Around these interface and AI-support conditions, the study should explicitly vary task context. Time pressure can be manipulated, for example, by changing the number of questions that must be completed within the available time, making full manual completion difficult in some conditions. Perceived AI competence can be shaped through a pre-task calibration phase in which participants see the assistant’s prior performance on similar tasks. Task stakes can be assessed by introducing reward/penalty schemes, e.g., where participants earn points for correct answers and lose a small number of points when they do not provide supporting evidence alongside the answers. These incentives to make the user’s choices more consequential and engaging ought to be introduced while making sure to keep the interaction between the user and the AI low-risk and non-harmful from an ethical standpoint.

paragraphs.en: The proposed design is different from work on cooperative question answering where delegation is observed mainly as the decision to let the AI answer on behalf of the team Gor et al. paragraphs.en: This paper started from an empirical study that deliberately focused on AI-literate users as an initial population for examining how post-interaction trust relates to intended delegation in repeated Video Question Answering tasks. In this context, the choice to verify the AI outputs remained common even when self-declared trust was high. This pattern suggests that trust is behaviourally consequential, but demands a more systematic study of how human oversight dynamics are embedded in everyday use. The graph comparison adds an XAI-specific observation. Inspectable and editable representations were actively used and were exploratorily associated with stronger intended delegation, while showing no reliable association with trust-delegation mismatch. Future evaluations should therefore examine whether graph inspection helps users identify incorrect relations, revise the represented evidence, and retain control when errors are detected.

paragraphs.en: We thus proposed a shift toward enacted delegation, providing a methodological bridge between subjective trust and human oversight. In this definition, we framed delegation as a traceable redistribution of responsibility across a task, allowing researchers to observe how much work is handed over, to what extent AI outputs are inspected, and whether control can be recovered after failure. This perspective is especially relevant for multimodal and agentic AI systems, where assistance increasingly involves interpreting heterogeneous evidence and acting across several steps of a workflow.

Empirically, we showed that intended delegation captures aspects of repeated human-AI interaction that cannot be reduced to trust ratings. Methodologically, we proposed a framework to be operationalised and validated in future studies of delegation as it is enacted in collaborative multimodal tasks, while controlling for time pressure, perceived AI competence, and task stakes. Although the empirical study began with AI-literate participants, the proposed framework is intended to support comparative studies across populations with different levels of AI familiarity and domain expertise.

Our broader aim is to encourage discussion on evaluating multimodal, explainable, and agentic AI systems in terms of the quality of oversight they support. Enacted delegation offers one way to make this quality observable by turning the small, distributed decisions through which users retain or transfer control in everyday AI use into a measurable object of human-centred interaction research.
